Part 1 of 7

Carter and the Rise of Reagan

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 1: Analyze what the successes and the failures of the Carter presidency were.

Core Objective 2: Identify the key factors that led to the election of Ronald Reagan, the rise of the modern conservative movement, and the resurgence of the Republican Party.

IN MY WORDS: Name one success and one failure of President Carter. Then name one group that helped Ronald Reagan win in 1980.

Reading ACarter’s Successes and Failures

During the first two years of his presidency, Jimmy Carter enjoyed several successes, both symbolic and real. . . . His administration included more African Americans and women than any before. . . . Ultimately, Carter’s inability to revive the economy crippled his presidency.

Jimmy Carter’s crowning achievement, which even his most bitter critics applauded, was his dogged effort to negotiate a 1978 peace agreement between Prime Minister Menachem Begin of Israel and President Anwar Sadat of Egypt. . . . It was the first time that an Arab nation (Egypt) had officially recognized the existence of Israel. However, this historic agreement—dubbed the Camp David Accords for the presidential retreat where the negotiations took place—created only a “framework for peace,” not a true settlement of differences.

Word help: symbolic = standing for an idea · revive = bring back to life · crippled = badly damaged · crowning achievement = greatest success · dogged = never giving up · framework = a basic plan

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “The Carter Presidency” (Early Success; Carter’s Limitations; Carter’s Foreign Policy) (pp. 1321–1323).

Reading BThe Iranian Hostage Crisis (1979)

On November 4, 1979, an Iranian mob stormed the U.S. embassy in Tehran and seized sixty-six diplomats, Marines, and staff, including fifty-two American citizens.

Iran released the hostages on Inauguration Day 1981, only hours after Ronald Reagan took office. The crisis had lasted for 444 days, all but ending Carter’s chances for reelection.

Word help: embassy = a nation’s official office in another country · seized = took by force · diplomats = officials who represent a country · hostages = people held as prisoners until demands are met · Inauguration Day = the day a new president takes office

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “The Carter Presidency” (Crisis in Iran) (pp. 1325–1327).

Reading CReagan and the Christian Right

Yet his promises of boundless economic expansion resonated with voters. By reducing taxes and easing government regulation of business, he argued, the engine of free-enterprise capitalism would spread wealth to everyone.

The California tax revolt fed into a national conservative resurgence led by the rapidly growing “Christian Right.” Religious conservatives promoting a faith-based political agenda formed the strongest grassroots movement of the late twentieth century.

On Election Day 1980, Reagan swept to a lopsided victory, with 489 electoral votes to 49 for Carter, who carried only six states . . . Reagan’s victory signaled a major realignment of voters in which many so-called Reagan Democrats—conservative White southern Protestants and working-class northern Catholics— voted for the Republican presidential candidate for the first time.

Word help: his = Ronald Reagan’s · resonated = connected with · regulation = government rules · resurgence = coming back stronger · grassroots = started by ordinary people · lopsided = very uneven · realignment = a big shift in which party people vote for

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “The Rise of Ronald Reagan” (The Candidate of Hope and Optimism; The Christian Right; The Election of 1980) (pp. 1328–1330).

Part 2 of 7

Reaganomics and the End of the Cold War

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 3: Define “Reaganomics” and evaluate its effects on American society and economy.

Core Objective 4: Explain how Reagan’s Soviet strategy helped end the Cold War.

IN MY WORDS: What was Reaganomics? How did Reagan try to beat the Soviet Union?

Reading DReaganomics

On August 1, 1981, President Reagan signed the Economic Recovery Tax Act (ERTA), which cut personal income taxes by 25 percent, lowered the maximum tax rate from 70 to 50 percent for 1982, and offered a broad array of tax concessions. . . . While theorists called the philosophy behind the plan “supply-side economics,” journalists dubbed the president’s proposals Reaganomics.

The solution, according to Reagan, was to slash tax rates, especially on the wealthy, in the belief that they would spend their tax savings on business expansion and consumer goods (the “supply side” of the economy). Such spending, Reagan and others believed, would provide “trickle-down” benefits to the masses.

In the short term, however, ERTA did not work as planned. The federal budget deficit grew, and by November 1981, the economy was officially in recession. . . . The federal deficit almost tripled during Reagan’s two terms.

Word help: ERTA = Economic Recovery Tax Act · concessions = breaks or favors · slash = cut sharply · trickle-down = flowing down slowly from the rich to everyone else · the masses = ordinary people · deficit = the amount the government spends beyond what it takes in

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “The Reagan Revolution” (Reaganomics; Managing the Budget; Reagan’s Half-Hearted Revolution) (pp. 1332–1335).

Reading EReagan, Gorbachev, and the Arms Race

Reagan claimed that such massive military spending would bankrupt the Soviets by forcing them to spend much more on their own military budgets.

In 1983, Reagan escalated the nuclear arms race by authorizing the Defense Department to develop the controversial Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), featuring a complex antimissile defense system that used satellites with laser weapons to “intercept and destroy” Soviet missiles in flight.

Under Mikhail Gorbachev, who became the Soviet leader in 1985, the Soviets renewed the policy of détente, encouraging a reduction of tensions with the United States. . . . After nine months of strenuous negotiations, Reagan and Gorbachev met amid much fanfare in Washington, D.C., on December 9, 1987, and signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty, an agreement to eliminate thousands of intermediate-range (300- to 3,000-mile) missiles.

Word help: bankrupt = make someone run out of money · escalated = made bigger · antimissile = stopping missiles · intercept = stop on the way · Gorbachev = the leader of the Soviet Union after 1985 · détente = easing of tensions · treaty = a formal agreement between countries

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “An Anti-Communist Foreign Policy” (A Massive Defense Buildup; A Historic Treaty; The INF Treaty) (pp. 1336–1340).

Source F“Tear Down This Wall” (Primary Source)

In June 1987, President Reagan gave a speech in Berlin, Germany, next to the Berlin Wall. The wall split Communist East Berlin from free West Berlin. Norton writes that Reagan “called upon the Soviet Union to allow greater freedom in Eastern European countries under its control.”

“General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, if you seek liberalization: Come here to this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!”

Word help: General Secretary = the title of the Soviet leader · seek = look for · prosperity = wealth and success · liberalization = more freedom

Ronald Reagan, speech at the Brandenburg Gate, Berlin, June 12, 1987. Quoted in Norton, Ch. 29, “An Anti-Communist Foreign Policy” (Reagan in Berlin) (p. 1340).

Source F. What did Reagan ask Gorbachev to do? What three things did Reagan say Gorbachev would get if he did it?

Point of view. Norton calls the speech “great theater—and good politics.” Who was Reagan really speaking to, and why would this speech help him?

Reading GThe Iran–Contra Affair (1987)

At the center of what came to be called the Iran–Contra affair was Marine Lieutenant Colonel Oliver North, a swashbuckling aide to the National Security Council who specialized in counterterrorism. Working from the basement of the White House, North had been secretly selling military supplies to Iran and using the proceeds to provide weapons to the Contra rebels fighting in Nicaragua—at a time when Congress had voted to ban such aid.

Word help: swashbuckling = bold and daring · counterterrorism = fighting terrorists · proceeds = money earned from a sale · Contra rebels = fighters trying to overthrow Nicaragua’s left-wing government · ban = forbid

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “An Anti-Communist Foreign Policy” (The Iran–Contra Affair) (p. 1338).

Part 3 of 7

The 1980s and a World after the Cold War

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 5: Characterize the economic and social issues and innovations that emerged during the 1980s.

Core Objective 6: Appraise the impact of the end of the Cold War and the efforts of President George H. W. Bush to create a post–Cold War foreign policy.

IN MY WORDS: Name one new invention and one social problem of the 1980s. Then name one big event that ended the Cold War.

Reading HA Changing Economy and the AIDS Epidemic

In the 1980s, computers became tools that everyone sought for a variety of purposes. . . . Despite unprecedented prosperity in the 1980s, homelessness became the most acute and visible social issue. An estimated 400,000 people were dispossessed by the end of the decade.

The Reagan administration showed little interest in AIDS because it was initially viewed as a “gay” disease. . . . Buchanan and others convinced Reagan not to address the HIV/AIDS issue, and even though millions of people—not solely gays—were at risk, there was little funding for medical research. As a result, by 2000, AIDS had terrorized the gay community and become the leading cause of death among men ages twenty-five to forty-four.

Word help: acute = serious · dispossessed = left without a home · Buchanan = Patrick Buchanan, Reagan’s communications director · HIV/AIDS = a deadly disease that attacks the body’s defenses

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “The Changing Economic and Social Landscape” (The Computer Revolution; The Poor; The AIDS Epidemic) (pp. 1340–1345).

Reading IThe Cold War Ends

In the Soviet Union, amazing changes were under way. In December 1988, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev shocked the world by announcing a series of far-reaching reforms such as perestroika (Russian for “economic restructuring”) and glasnost (“openness”), a loosening of centralized economic planning and censorship of the press.

The most spectacular event in the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe came on November 9, 1989. . . . Soon Germans on both sides—using hand tools and even their bare hands—tore down the wall, the chief symbol of the Cold War.

Four months later, on December 25, 1991, Gorbachev resigned and handed governing authority to Boris Yeltsin. That evening, the Soviet flag was lowered from the Kremlin and replaced with the Russian flag.

Word help: perestroika = economic restructuring · glasnost = openness · censorship = the government blocking what can be printed or said · collapse = fall apart · Yeltsin = Boris Yeltsin, leader of Russia · the Kremlin = the seat of the Soviet government in Moscow

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “George H. W. Bush and the Reagan Legacy” (The Democracy Movement Abroad; The End of the Berlin Wall; Soviet Coup Fails) (pp. 1350–1351).

Picture 1A Hammer to the Soviet Empire

In November 1989, the Berlin Wall began to come down. Norton’s caption: “A West German demonstrator pounding away at the heavily graffitied Berlin Wall with a sledgehammer. East Berlin border guards look on from atop the wall.” (Primary source.)

What to look for: demonstrator = a protester · graffitied = covered with spray paint · sledgehammer = a big, heavy hammer · border guards = soldiers who guarded the wall · atop = on top of

Norton, Ch. 29, “George H. W. Bush and the Reagan Legacy,” Visual Explorations: “A Hammer to the Soviet Empire” (p. 1351). Primary source (photograph, 1989).

Picture 1. (1) What is the man doing? (2) What are the East Berlin guards on top of the wall doing? (3) Why would Norton call the photo “A Hammer to the Soviet Empire”?

Reading JOperation Desert Storm (1991)

In August 1990, Saddam Hussein, dictator of Iraq, invaded Kuwait, its tiny but oil-rich neighbor, sparking the first major international crisis of the post–Cold War era.

Four days later, U.S. military units and those from thirty-three other nations, including ten Islamist countries, launched Operation Desert Storm against Iraq. During the next six weeks, Iraqi soldiers surrendered by the thousands; and on February 28, Bush called for a cease-fire. . . . Although coalition forces occupied about one-fifth of Iraq, Hussein’s tyrannical regime remained intact.

Word help: dictator = a ruler with total power · Islamist = following a strict political form of Islam · cease-fire = an agreement to stop fighting · coalition = a group of nations working together · intact = still in place

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “George H. W. Bush and the Reagan Legacy” (The Gulf War) (p. 1353).

Clinton, a Changing Population, and 9/11

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 7: Evaluate the accomplishments and setbacks of Bill Clinton’s presidency.

Core Objective 8: Describe the major population trends (demographics) in the United States during the twenty-first century, and assess their impact on the nation’s politics.

Core Objective 9: Summarize the impact of global terrorism on the United States and the effectiveness of President George W. Bush in dealing with it.

IN MY WORDS: Give one success and one setback for Clinton. How is America’s population changing? How did the United States respond to 9/11?

Reading KThe Clinton Years

He served three more terms as Arkansas governor and in the process emerged as a dynamic young leader of the “New Democrats” who were committed to winning back the middle-class Whites (“Reagan Democrats”) that had voted Republican during the 1980s.

In 1994, Clinton urged Congress to approve NAFTA, which would make North America the largest free-trade zone in the world. . . . In the most astonishing congressional victory of the twentieth century, Republicans captured both houses of Congress for the first time since 1953. . . . He and his congressional colleagues promised to bring forward a Contract with America, an audacious pledge to dismantle the “corrupt liberal welfare state.”

Another feature of the new economy was globalization—the process by which people, goods, information, and cultural tastes circulated across national boundaries. . . . For all his faults, Bill Clinton presided over an unprecedented period of peace and prosperity (115 consecutive months of economic growth and the lowest unemployment rate in thirty years), generated record federal budget surpluses, and passed a welfare reform measure with support from both parties.

Word help: He served = Bill Clinton served · He and his congressional colleagues = Newt Gingrich, a Republican leader in Congress, and other Republicans · NAFTA = North American Free Trade Agreement (United States, Canada, and Mexico) · free-trade zone = an area where goods are traded with few taxes · audacious = very bold · dismantle = take apart · welfare state = government programs that help the poor · surpluses = more money coming in than going out

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “George H. W. Bush and the Reagan Legacy” (A New Democrat) (p. 1354). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 29, “The Clinton Presidency (1993–2001)” (The Economy; The Contract with America; Globalization; Assessing the Clinton Presidency) (pp. 1357–1366).

Reading LAmerica’s Changing Population

During the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, the United States experienced a historic third wave of immigration. . . . For the first time, most immigrants came not from Europe but from Asia, Latin America, and Africa.

In 2005, Hispanics (the term used by the U.S. Census Bureau) surpassed African Americans as the nation’s largest minority group. Yet Asian Americans were the fastest-growing racial or ethnic group in the United States.

These broad demographic shifts would also impact national election campaign strategies and electoral results, with longtime red states such as Georgia and Arizona now moving into the swing-state category.

Word help: third wave = the third big period of immigration in U.S. history · minority group = a group that is less than half the population · demographic = about the makeup of the population · red states = states that usually vote Republican · swing state = a state that could vote for either party

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 30, “The Third Wave of Immigration and America’s Changing Population” (pp. 1372–1374).

Reading M9/11 and the War on Terror

Early on the morning of September 11, 2001, Islamist terrorists hijacked four U.S. airliners filled with passengers. . . . The war on terror, Bush stressed, would begin with al Qaeda but would “not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped, and defeated.”

At the same time, Bush convinced Congress to approve the USA Patriot Act (2001), which gave government agencies authority to eavesdrop on confidential conversations between prison inmates and their lawyers. . . . Civil liberties groups voiced concerns that the measures jeopardized constitutional rights and protections, but most Americans supported those measures.

The Bush Doctrine declared that the growing menace posed by “shadowy networks” of terrorist groups and unstable rogue nations with weapons of mass destruction (WMD) required the United States at times to use preemptive military action and to act unilaterally if necessary to eliminate the threats of hostile nations such as Iraq using WMD.

Word help: hijacked = took control of by force · al Qaeda = the terrorist group behind 9/11 · eavesdrop = secretly listen · civil liberties = basic freedoms protected by the Constitution · rogue nations = countries that break international rules · preemptive = striking first · unilaterally = alone, without allies

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 30, “A Chaotic Start to a New Century” (9/11—A New Day of Infamy; The War on Terror; Fighting Terror at Home; The Bush Doctrine) (pp. 1376–1379).

Obama and Trump

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 10: Describe the factors that contributed to Barack Obama’s groundbreaking victory in the 2008 presidential election.

Core Objective 11: Identify President Obama’s policy priorities at home and abroad, and assess his efforts to pursue them.

Core Objective 12: Describe the defining aspects of Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign and his subsequent presidency.

IN MY WORDS: Name one reason Obama won in 2008, one thing he did as president, and one thing that made Trump’s 2016 campaign different.

Reading NThe Great Recession and the 2008 Election

Yet TARP, while shoring up the large financial institutions, did little to restore the public’s confidence in the economy—or to stem what would come to be called the Great Recession.

As the primaries played out, however, an overconfident Clinton lost the nomination to Barack Obama of Illinois, who, though only a first-term senator, was a groundbreaking candidate in his own right: the most competitive African American candidate for a presidential nomination that the country had ever seen. . . . Obama and his strategists mastered the use of social media to organize rock-concert–like campaign rallies.

On November 4, 2008, Obama made history by becoming the first person of color to be elected president. . . . Voter turnout, especially among African Americans and young adults, was the highest since 1968.

He had also faced an array of other challenges: continuing turmoil in Iraq, a devastating storm on the Gulf coast, and the widespread economic shock of the Great Recession. These issues and the government response led a number of voters to abandon Republican governance to seek new leadership under a Democratic president.

Word help: TARP = a 2008 law that spent $700 billion to keep big banks from failing · shoring up = holding up · stem = stop · Great Recession = the deep economic downturn that began in 2007 · primaries = elections to pick each party’s candidate · Clinton = Hillary Clinton, a senator from New York · turnout = how many people vote · He = President George W. Bush · abandon = leave

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 30, “Second-Term Blues” (Economic Shock: The Great Recession; A Groundbreaking New Presidency; The First African American President) (pp. 1384–1386).

MapMap 30.3: The Election of 2008

This modern textbook map shows which candidate won each state in 2008 and how many electoral votes each state had.

Map key: Blue = won by Barack Obama (Democrat) · Orange = won by John McCain (Republican) · number in each state = its electoral votes · popular vote = the total number of people who voted for each candidate

Norton, Ch. 30, Map 30.3, “The Election of 2008” (p. 1386). Modern textbook map.

Map evidence. (1) How many electoral votes did each candidate win? (2) Name two southern states Obama won. (3) Use Reading N: give two reasons Obama won.

Reading OObama in Office

The president’s goal in creating the Affordable Care Act (ACA), which critics called Obamacare, was to make health insurance more affordable and health care more accessible.

On May 1, 2011, President Obama authorized a daring night raid by a Navy SEAL team transported by helicopters from Afghanistan. After a brief firefight, the SEALs killed bin Laden. . . . Soon, the revolt became a national Tea Party movement, with chapters in all fifty states.

Also in 2012, President Obama became the first sitting president to support the right of gay and lesbian couples to marry. . . . In 2013, three African American activists—Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors, and Opal Tometi—created a civil rights organization called Black Lives Matter (BLM) to address mounting evidence that African Americans were being treated unfairly by law enforcement officers and the judicial system.

Word help: affordable = not too expensive · accessible = easy to get · bin Laden = Osama bin Laden, leader of al Qaeda · revolt = here, a protest by conservatives against Obama’s spending and taxes · judicial system = the courts

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 30, “The Obama Administration” (Health-Care Reform; The Death of Osama bin Laden; The Tea Party Movement; Marriage Equality; Black Lives Matter) (pp. 1388–1396).

Reading PThe Trump Presidency

The politics of grievance proved crucial to the unprecedented presidential campaign of Donald Trump, a celebrity real-estate developer and reality-television star who had never held elected office.

Trump’s campaign also benefited from the surging influence of social media platforms such as Twitter (now called “X”) and Facebook. . . . And candidate Trump relentlessly used Twitter, sending dozens of daily tweets to his growing number of followers.

Perhaps Trump’s greatest success was the appointment of three conservative justices to the Supreme Court: Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett. . . . In March 2018, in an effort to promote economic nationalism, protect domestic producers, and live up to his populist campaign promise to “Make America Great Again,” President Trump announced tariffs on imported steel and aluminum.

After fiery debate, the Democratic-controlled House passed two articles of impeachment, charging Trump with abuse of power and obstruction of Congress. . . . On February 5, 2020, the Senate found Trump not guilty by a vote of 48–52, with all 47 Senate Democrats voting guilty on both counts.

Word help: grievance = a feeling of being treated unfairly · unprecedented = never happened before · relentlessly = without stopping · populist = claiming to speak for ordinary people against elites · tariffs = taxes on imported goods · impeached = charged with wrongdoing by the House

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 30, “The Trump Administration” (The Politics of Grievance; Trump and Social Media; Court Appointments; Launching a Trade War; First Impeachment) (pp. 1400–1412).

Pandemic, Biden, and a Divided Nation

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 13: Assess the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and racial justice protests on the nation and the 2020 presidential election.

Core Objective 14: Identify the domestic and foreign policy challenges that the Biden administration faced, and assess its policy responses.

Core Objective 15: Describe how deepening political polarization was evident in the 2024 presidential campaign.

IN MY WORDS: How did the COVID-19 pandemic and the George Floyd protests affect the country? What is political polarization?

Reading QThe Pandemic, Protests, and the 2020 Election

Still, the 2019–2021 pandemic had a colossal effect on daily life throughout the world. . . . With less than 5 percent of the world’s population, the United States had 25 percent of the world’s confirmed coronavirus cases.

Amid the pandemic, more highly publicized killings of African Americans by White police officers and White supremacists ignited a wave of racial justice protests nationwide.

He beat President Trump by 52 to 47 percent in the popular vote, with a winning margin of more than 7 million votes nationwide. The Electoral College tally was 306 votes for Biden and 232 for Trump . . . The COVID-19 pandemic, rather than being a shared burden that brought people together, had tended only to enflame existing cultural and political divisions.

Word help: pandemic = a disease that spreads around the world · colossal = huge · coronavirus = the virus that causes COVID-19 · publicized = shown in the news · racial justice = fair treatment for all races · He = Joe Biden · enflame = make worse

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 30, “Sideswiped by a Pandemic” (Global Impact; Health Impact of the Pandemic; George Floyd Racial Justice Protests; Extended Vote Count) (pp. 1414–1424).

Reading RBiden and Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022)

Just two months into his presidency, Biden signed the American Rescue Plan, a COVID-19 relief package that was widely popular with people still struggling with the pandemic’s effects.

In terms of foreign policy, President Biden had mixed success. . . . The withdrawal proved utterly chaotic. Taliban forces advanced far more quickly than anyone had imagined that they would.

In a landmark 6–3 decision, the Court’s conservative majority overturned Roe, ruling that access to abortion is not a right guaranteed under the Constitution. Dobbs returned to the individual states the right to regulate abortion access.

By April 2023, his job approval ratings had dropped to 37 percent, down twenty points from when he took office. Rising inflation played the largest role in this decline.

Word help: relief package = a law that gives money to help people · withdrawal = here, U.S. troops leaving Afghanistan · chaotic = in total disorder · Taliban = the group that took over Afghanistan · landmark = very important · overturned Roe = ended the 1973 Roe v. Wade ruling · inflation = rising prices

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 30, “The Biden Presidency” (Biden’s Domestic Agenda; Biden’s Foreign Policy; The Politics of Abortion; Growing Dissatisfaction) (pp. 1425–1430).

Reading SThe 2024 Campaign and Political Polarization

It was inevitable because polarization had become so deeply entrenched in American politics. Both parties cast the election as one of doom and despair if their side did not win.

On July 21, Biden surprised the country by releasing a letter to the press announcing that he was resigning from the race. He then endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris to take his place.

With his two and a half million vote advantage, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate to win the popular vote in twenty years. His margin in the Electoral College was more comfortable: 312 electoral votes to Harris’s 226.

In this excerpt, Jonathan Haidt, a prominent social psychologist and author, argues that social media has played a particularly important role in the rise of political polarization.

Word help: inevitable = sure to happen · polarization = splitting into two opposite sides · entrenched = dug in, hard to change · endorsed = publicly supported · Haidt = Jonathan Haidt, a social psychologist

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 30, “The 2024 Presidential Campaign” (pp. 1431–1433). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 30, “The Biden Presidency” (Comparing Perspectives: Political Polarization in Modern America) (pp. 1428–1429).

From 1977 to 2024, did conservatives or liberals do more to shape modern America?

ClaimAnswer the question in one sentence.
EvidenceTwo specific facts (dates, events, numbers).
ReasoningHow do the facts prove your claim?
